1842–1910 · United States

William James

American physician, psychologist and philosopher. His Principles of Psychology (1890) described consciousness as a stream and shaped generations of readers.

Biography

William James was born in New York in 1842 into a cultured, much-travelled family; his brother Henry became a celebrated novelist. He tried painting, studied chemistry and medicine at Harvard, taking his medical degree in 1869, and went through a long period of personal crisis and ill health. At Harvard he began by teaching physiology and moved into psychology; around 1875 he set up a room there for experimental demonstrations. By his own account, the first psychology lecture he ever heard was the first one he gave.

He took twelve years to finish The Principles of Psychology (1890), two volumes still read for their clarity and style. He then devoted himself increasingly to philosophy. He died in 1910 in Chocorua, New Hampshire.

Questions he investigated

  • What is consciousness for? What role does it play in adaptation?
  • How are habits formed and maintained?
  • Do we feel afraid and therefore tremble, or tremble and therefore feel afraid?
  • What do the religious experiences of very different people have in common?

Contributions

James described consciousness not as a chain of elements but as a continuous, personal and selective stream. At the same time as the Danish physician Carl Lange, he proposed that emotion is the perception of bodily changes (the James–Lange theory). His chapters on habit, attention and the self influenced functionalist psychology, education and pragmatist philosophy.

Collaborations, influences and disagreements

He admired and argued with Wundt; he supported his student Mary Whiton Calkins, whom Harvard refused a doctorate because she was a woman; and he taught G. Stanley Hall, who earned his doctorate under him. He kept up an intellectual friendship with Charles S. Peirce and John Dewey.

Criticism, limits and reception

The James–Lange theory was criticised in 1927 by Walter Cannon and Philip Bard, who pointed out that bodily responses are too slow and too unspecific to explain different emotions. Current theories combine bodily feedback with cognitive appraisal and context. His interest in the psychical research of his day was also controversial.

References

  1. James, W. (1890). The Principles of Psychology. Nueva York: Henry Holt.
  2. Richardson, R. D. (2006). William James: In the Maelstrom of American Modernism. Boston: Houghton Mifflin.
  3. Cannon, W. B. (1927). The James-Lange theory of emotions: a critical examination. American Journal of Psychology, 39, 106–124.
